name: Grunwald
kingdom: Kingdom of Poland / Grand Duchy of Lithuania
summary: A Masurian village that gave its Polish name to the battle of 15 July 1410 — one of three villages around a field whose exact position is still argued over.
overview: A village in Masuria beside the field where Polish-Lithuanian forces destroyed the army of the Teutonic Order in 1410.
knownFor: The field of 15 July 1410, one of the largest battles of medieval Europe
Three villages and three names: Grunwald, Tannenberg (Stębark) and Žalgiris
A memorial landscape of 1960 with a chapel site, mass graves and a battlefield museum

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Grunwald is a village in the Warmian-Masurian voivodeship of northern Poland, in the district of Ostróda, with about four hundred inhabitants. It was called Grünfelde until 1945. Nothing about the place would be remembered except that on 15 July 1410 the army of Władysław II Jagiełło and Vytautas destroyed the field army of the Teutonic Order somewhere in the four square kilometres of rolling farmland around it.

The village is therefore a battlefield rather than a town, and almost everything a visitor sees — an obelisk, a museum, the excavated footings of a chapel, a line of flagpoles — was put there to mark the day rather than to serve the place.

contentSections.title: Three villages, three names
paragraphs: The fighting took place on the ground between three settlements: Grunwald (Grünfelde), Stębark (Tannenberg) and Łodwigowo (Ludwigsdorf). Each of the three nations involved named the battle after a different one of them, which is why the same engagement appears in the literature under three names — Grunwald in Polish, Tannenberg in German, and Žalgiris in Lithuanian, the last a translation of the same "green wood" that lies behind the German and Polish forms.

The naming is not a curiosity but a live political fact. Because the German tradition attached itself to Tannenberg, the name was deliberately reused in 1914 for a victory fought in the same region, explicitly presented as an answer to 1410 — five centuries of grievance retrieved by choosing a place name.

contentSections.title: Where exactly the battle was fought
paragraphs: The traditional placing of the field goes back to Jan Długosz’s narrative and to a map published by Johannes Voigt in 1836, and it is where the memorial complex stands. That placing is not secure. In 2009 the Swedish historian Sven Ekdahl argued that the main fighting took place elsewhere on the ground — north-east of the road between Grunwald and Łodwigowo, roughly two kilometres south-west of the memorial — and the question has not been settled since.

Between 2014 and 2019 Scandinavian and Polish archaeologists surveyed some 450 hectares with metal detectors and recovered about 1,500 objects, of which perhaps 150 relate to the battle: crossbow bolts, arrowheads, spurs and Teutonic coins with Gothic inscriptions. The surveys have been criticised for inconsistent method and incomplete recording, and they have narrowed the argument rather than closed it. The honest position is that the battle happened within this landscape and that the precise field is still contested.

contentSections.title: The chapel and the graves
paragraphs: The Teutonic Order marked the ground itself. Grand Master Heinrich von Plauen had a chapel dedicated to Saint Mary built on the battlefield, consecrated in March 1413, standing over the dead of the side that lost. It was destroyed in the Hunger War of 1414, rebuilt, allowed to decay after the Reformation and finally demolished in 1720.

Excavation around the chapel ruins between 1958 and 1960 found what the chapel had been built for: burial pits beside it holding the remains of more than 250 people, with further graves in the neighbouring villages of Dąbrówno and Ulnowo, many of the bones showing weapon injuries. These are the most direct physical evidence for the battle that exists, and they anchor the memorial site to the traditional field even while the exact line of fighting is argued.

contentSections.title: The battlefield since 1960
paragraphs: The present memorial was built in 1960 for the 550th anniversary, north-east of the chapel ruins, to a design by the sculptor Jerzy Bandura and the architect Witold Cęckiewicz: an obelisk, eleven flagpoles thirty metres high, and a sculptural map showing the positions of the armies. A battlefield museum of some 275 square metres displays the excavated finds, reconstructed banners, weapons and maps, and construction of a larger year-round museum began in April 2019.

The site was designated a Historic Monument of Poland on 4 October 2010, and the anniversary is marked on the ground each July. In July 2020, for the 610th anniversary, the Polish and Lithuanian presidents unveiled a commemorative stone carved with the Vytis, the Lithuanian mounted knight — the two states that fought here together still commemorating it together.

timeline.title: The battle
timeline.description: Polish and Lithuanian forces under Władysław II Jagiełło and Vytautas destroy the Teutonic field army; Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen is killed.

timeline.title: The Order’s chapel consecrated
timeline.description: Heinrich von Plauen has a chapel of Saint Mary consecrated on the battlefield over the graves of the defeated.

timeline.title: Chapel destroyed
timeline.description: The chapel is destroyed during the Hunger War and afterwards rebuilt.

timeline.title: Chapel demolished
timeline.description: After decay following the Reformation, the battlefield chapel is finally pulled down.

timeline.title: Voigt’s map
timeline.description: Johannes Voigt publishes the map that fixes the traditional location of the field for more than a century.

timeline.title: The mass graves excavated
timeline.description: Digging around the chapel ruins uncovers burial pits with the remains of more than 250 people, many showing weapon injuries.

timeline.title: The memorial raised
timeline.description: For the 550th anniversary, Jerzy Bandura and Witold Cęckiewicz build the obelisk, flagpoles and sculptural map that define the site today.

timeline.title: The site questioned
timeline.description: Sven Ekdahl argues that the main fighting lay about two kilometres south-west of the memorial; the question remains open.

timeline.title: Historic Monument of Poland
timeline.description: The battlefield is given Poland’s highest heritage designation.
